title: Learn about yearly charity (zakat) and the pilgrimage (Hajj)
whyMatters: Zakat (charitable giving) and Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca) are two of the five pillars, and once you understand them you have the whole foundation of what being Muslim involves. Zakat purifies your wealth and keeps the community looking after the people in need. Hajj is a once-in-a-lifetime trip to the House of Allah in Mecca, where millions of Muslims from every part of the world stand together, and it tends to change people. Both are longer-term commitments and neither one is urgent. Learning about them now is groundwork for later.

subSteps: Zakat is an obligatory annual charity of 2.5% of your savings and qualifying wealth.

It is due once your wealth passes a minimum threshold called the nisab. Nisab is a weight of gold or silver (Islamic Relief Canada gives 87.48 grams of gold or 612.36 grams of silver), so its dollar value changes with metal prices. Charities use slightly different figures.
The wealth has to have been held for one full lunar year (hawl) before Zakat is due on it.
It is calculated on savings, investments, gold, silver, and business assets. Your home, your car, and your everyday belongings are not counted.
It goes to eight categories of people named in the Quran (9:60), including the poor, people in debt, and travelers who are stranded.
Many Muslims pay their Zakat during Ramadan, though it can be paid at any time of year.

exactActions.text: Learn how to calculate your Zakat
subSteps: Add up your total qualifying wealth: savings accounts, cash, investments, gold, silver, and business inventory.
Subtract debts that are due now. Charities and scholars treat long-term debts such as a mortgage or student loan differently, so ask.
If what is left is above the nisab threshold, pay 2.5% of that total as Zakat.
Canadian charities such as National Zakat Foundation Canada and Muslim Welfare Canada publish calculators. They use slightly different nisab figures, so results can differ.
Keep your first year simple and stick to cash savings. The finer details can wait until your finances get more complicated.
Alongside obligatory Zakat, Islam strongly encourages voluntary giving, called Sadaqah.
Sadaqah can be money, and it can also be a kind word, helping someone carry their groceries, or smiling at somebody.
The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Every act of goodness is charity' (Sahih Muslim 1005).
You can give Sadaqah at any time, in any amount, to anyone in need.

Get into the habit of giving regularly, even if the amounts are small. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said the deeds Allah loves most are the regular ones, even if they are few (Sahih al-Bukhari 6464).
Hajj is a pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia, that every Muslim must make once in their lifetime if they are physically and financially able.
It falls in the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah and lasts five to six days.
Pilgrims wear plain white garments (ihram), which put everyone on the same footing before Allah whatever their wealth or status.
The rituals include circling the Ka'bah (tawaf), walking between the hills of Safa and Marwa, standing at the plain of Arafat, and the symbolic stoning of the devil.
Hajj ends with Eid al-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, which Muslims celebrate worldwide.
Ask anyone who has been, and most will tell you nothing else in their life compares.
Nobody is pushing you to go now. Many Muslims save for years first.
Hajj becomes obligatory only when you are physically and financially able, meaning you can afford it without shortchanging your own needs or the people who depend on you.

Before you plan, check the Government of Canada's travel advice for Saudi Arabia on travel.gc.ca, because the advisory level changes. When we checked on September 23, 2026, the page (last updated September 17, 2026) advised avoiding non-essential travel to Saudi Arabia.

Hajj needs a Hajj visa and a booking through the official Nusuk Hajj platform, which sells packages from authorised service providers. Nusuk listed Canada among its serviced countries for the 2026 season. Check whether it does for the year you plan, and remember that registering does not guarantee a place.
In the meantime, Umrah (the lesser pilgrimage) can be done at any time of year, and travel.gc.ca says it can be done on any visa type.
Open a Hajj savings fund, even for a small amount each month. It adds up.
Read about Hajj, watch documentaries, and listen to people who have been. It gets you ready long before you go.

timeEstimate: Zakat is worked out once a year when it applies. Hajj is a goal you build towards over years

obstacles.problem: I don't know how to calculate my Zakat
obstacles.solution: Zakat looks complicated and then turns out to be one line: qualifying wealth, minus debts that are due, times 2.5%. Several Canadian charities publish free calculators and guidance, and the zakat guide on this site explains the terms. For your first year, a reasonable estimate made in good faith is perfectly acceptable, and a qualified scholar can check it.

obstacles.problem: Hajj feels impossible, it's so far away and expensive
obstacles.solution: Plenty of Muslims feel this way, and it is a normal reaction. Hajj is a big undertaking and it was always meant to be. Start by learning about it and letting the idea settle in you. The obligation only lands once you are physically and financially able, so there is no guilt in waiting. Open a savings account for it and put in what you can. Some people go in their twenties and others in their sixties. Allah knows your intention and your circumstances.

obstacles.problem: I have financial concerns about giving Zakat
obstacles.solution: Zakat is only obligatory if your wealth sits above the nisab threshold. If it is below, zakat is not due from you, and if you are struggling you may be able to receive it. Even when it is due, 2.5% of savings is meant to be manageable. Islam does not ask you for more than you can give. If your situation is unclear, talk to a knowledgeable imam or a Zakat advisor at a charity you trust.

obstacles.problem: I don't know where to give my Zakat
obstacles.solution: Choose a registered charity that is open about where the money goes, and check it on the Canada Revenue Agency's list of charities first. The zakat guide on this site lists some Canadian charities with their registration numbers, without endorsing any of them. You can also give directly to people in need: widows, orphans, people in debt, students. Your masjid may run a Zakat distribution program as well.

obstacles.problem: I feel disconnected from Hajj since I've never been to Mecca
obstacles.solution: You can build the connection long before you go. Watch documentaries about the pilgrimage. Read accounts from converts who have performed Hajj. Learn the history of the Ka'bah and the story of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his family, whose legacy the Hajj rituals honor. Every time you pray facing the qiblah you are already turning towards the Ka'bah. The connection exists now, from wherever you happen to be standing.

tinyVersion: Zakat is 2.5% of your savings, given once a year to people in need. Hajj is a once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage to Mecca, for when you are able. Both sit in the future, so learn about them now and plan when you are ready.
unlocksNext: With all five pillars in view, Shahada, Salah, Sawm, Zakat, and Hajj, you have the whole foundation. From here it is about living it, day after ordinary day.
